l: A. Procurement and Storage of Unassigned Armor

1. The Police Training Division shall coordinate procurement and issuance of new and replacement body armor for all divisions with the assistance of Police Procurement, the Body Armor Coordinator, and Unit Personnel. Asset Management shall be tasked with recording asset data into the MCM System and with storing unassigned body armor. The supply and inventory shall be controlled by Asset Management in coordination with the Police Training Division personnel. Each assigned person will be responsible for the proper storage of the body armor and the Body Armor Database has accurate warranty information for their body armor. Asset Management, in coordination with the Police Training Division personnel, shall keep all necessary records on inventory, issues, and returns.

2. Officers wearing body armor with warranty that is expired shall report to Police Training Division for replacement. Replacement needed prior to warranty expiration should be accompanied by a replacement form documenting the reason(s) for replacement. Upon receipt of body armor, officers are to comply with regulations specifying usage of body armor as outlined below.

3. Unassigned body armor (and vests) shall be turned in to Asset Management, unless it is being held for a vacant position. Armor held for vacant positions should be turned in to Asset Management when the position(s) is filled but the person required a different fit. Asset Management and Training Division shall endeavor to utilize unassigned body armor whenever possible.
Unless an exception has been authorized by the Chief of Police, all sworn personnel shall wear body armor under the following conditions:
1. All uniformed personnel shall wear their issued body armor when:
b. Working a non-patrol assignment where their duties may require the officer to act in an enforcement capacity or while engaged in public activities.

c. Working an assignment that requires interaction with the public. This includes uniformed officers of any rank in administrative assignments whenever they leave their assignment and go into a public place.
2. All non-uniformed officers shall wear their issued body armor when:
a. Serving of a criminal warrant.
b. Planned apprehension of a wanted person.
c. Planned surveillance where an apprehension might logically occur.
d. While undercover and providing cover in field operations unless their position as an officer would be compromised.
e. Any other investigative assignment where the supervisor or the individual investigator concerned believes the armor should be worn.

Sworn personnel may elect not to wear protective armor under the below circumstances; however, an exception shall not relieve uniformed personnel of the responsibility to have their vest readily available and immediately accessible:

1. When exempt status has been granted in writing from the Chief of Police. Exempt status is a privilege granted by the Chief of Police, not an entitlement or a right and may be revoked at any time. Exemptions may include, but are not limited to:
a. Medical waiver issued by a physician, approved by the Chief of Police and filed with the Medical Records Custodian (MRC) in Police Employment Services.
b. When wearing the Class A dress uniform.
c. Any other situation the Chief of Police approves in writing.

D. To guard against the potential development of heat-related issues while wearing body armor, supervisors should be cognizant of particular assignments that may have abnormal heat or humid conditions. In such circumstances, supervisors should ensure their personnel have adequate breaks to cool down and remain hydrated. Officers should monitor their health and notify their supervisors of the need for breaks during such times.

1. Signs and symptoms of heat-related illness vary based on the condition, but may include an elevated body temperature, headache, nausea, weakness, dizziness, fainting, excessive sweating, fast heartbeat, muscle cramps, seizures, confusion, and coma.

3. The Training Captain is responsible for the appointment of the Body Armor Coordinator, which shall be a collateral duty for a sworn officer.

1. Asset Inventory – List of all department assets maintained by Asset Management for the purposes of the annual inventory. It includes asset data tracked by each Division. Items should have an individual cost of $500 or more and three (3) or more years of usable life.
2. Unit Asset Inventory – Unit’s list of assets that are required to be tracked for the annual inventory, equipment replacement, and inspections.

3.Replacement Schedule – Included in the unit’s asset inventory, this is a list of standard issue equipment scheduled for replacement that has an individual cost of $500 or more and three (3) or more years of usable life.

4. Special-Use/Periodic Use Equipment - Equipment not assigned to individual members of the department and includes, but is not limited to, special-use vehicles, equipment, supplies for special events or disasters, or specialized investigative equipment.

5. Standard Issue Equipment – Any equipment assigned to a division that is approved to be assigned to a replacement schedule. Items should have an individual cost of $500 or more and three (3) or more years of usable life.
6. Ad Hoc Equipment – Any equipment assigned to a division that is not approved to be on a replacement schedule. Items should have an individual cost of $500 or more and three
(3) or more years of usable life.
7. Equipment Manager – Position assigned by each division to track equipment for inventory and replacement.
8. Financial Liability Form – Form completed by equipment manager or supervisor for inventory items that are lost.

1. Each unit shall maintain a Unit Asset Inventory list of equipment assets. This list shall include both Replacement Schedule Equipment and Ad Hoc Equipment including equipment considered Special-Use/Periodic Use that must be available for inspection.

2. Assets with a cost of $500 or more and three (3) or more years of life shall also be listed in the department’s Asset Inventory maintained the MCM System database by the Asset Management Unit. This inventory should be updated at least annually during the department’s annual inventory reporting in August to ensure timely replacements can be scheduled. It is the responsibility of Asset Management to ensure that the information in the MCM system is accurate. Reports shall be available upon request.
3. Each unit’s asset list shall include both standard issue and ad hoc items:

a. Replacement Schedule Equipment - Items in the asset inventory that are approved as standard issue and may be assigned and unassigned equipment with an individual cost of $500 or more and three (3) or more years of usable life at purchase.

b. Ad Hoc Equipment – Items listed in the unit’s inventory list, including Special-Use/Periodic items, that are not considered standard issue. Ad hoc items may be subject to additional approvals and shall be replaced as funds are available.
c. Items not tracked in the unit’s inventory list
(1) Soft and Hard Armor - Vest equipment will be maintained by the Police Training Division.
(2) Fleet Equipment – Fleet assets that have both a motor AND license will be tracked by the Fleet Division. Trailers, golf carts, etc. shall be tracked for replacement by the assigned unit.
(3) Technology – Equipment issued by the City’s Information Technology Solutions (ITS) will be tracked by ITS.
(4) Radios – Radios issued by the ITS radio shop will be tracked by the radio shop.

4. Equipment items listed on each division’s replacement schedule shall be those approved by the Bureau as “standard issue.” Equipment that is not approved as standard issue shall be considered “ad hoc” for replacement purposes. Ad Hoc Equipment shall not be replaced through the same process as standard issue equipment. At the discretion of the chain of command, new and Ad Hoc Equipment purchases may be subject to an Equipment and Uniform committee review before being approved as standard issue and placed on the division’s replacement schedule.

5. The department shall create a centralized budget to ensure the timely replacement of standard issue equipment. The replacement of this equipment shall be on the basis of condition and with priority given to officer safety. In order to maintain the condition of standard issue equipment, command staff shall endeavor, when possible, to replace existing equipment before approving purchase of ad hoc or new equipment.

6. Each year, the list of replacement eligible equipment shall be submitted to command staff by Fiscal Command for prioritization. Following prioritization, units shall submit quotes to Fiscal Command to assess available budget for procurement.

7. Replacement equipment must be delivered to the Asset Management Unit in order to record the replaced equipment and dispose old equipment. Upon issuance to the unit, personnel must surrender the old equipment for disposal or categorized as ad hoc if it will be kept for redundancy purposes.
C. Uniform, Individually Assigned, and Personal Wear Items
1. Items Eligible for Replacement, if damaged while engaged in official capacity
a. Body armor that is five (5) years or older, no longer fits, or is in poor condition. TBP 7.23

b. Uniforms and leather goods that are damaged beyond repair and items required for a particular assignment such as western hats, special holsters, etc. which will be subject to the limit set by the Budget Section.

c. Prescription eyeglasses/contact lenses which will be limited only to the cost of lenses up to a $200 maximum and frames up to a $150 maximum, unless an exception is approved by the Chief of Police.
d. Watches up to a fifty-dollar (50) maximum.
e. Flashlights up to a fifty-dollar (50) maximum.

g. Miscellaneous items such as ticket book holders, personally-owned handheld radio holders, pens, sunglasses, etc., which shall be individually considered for replacement, up to a twenty-five-dollar (25) maximum, by the deputy chief subject to the on-duty damage guidelines.

2. For replacement of a personal item eligible for replacement, the officer shall prepare a replacement request with approval from their chain of command through the deputy chief, attach an inter-office correspondence and deliver the documents to the Budget Section for appropriate action.

3. No item, except body armor, shall be eligible for replacement due to wear-out. The officer shall prepare an Equipment Replacement Form and with approval of their chain of command deliver it to the Police Training Division for appropriate action. Items that are defective shall be returned to the vendor for replacement as part of the warranty process.
c. Footwear, unless issued by the police department for the assignment.
d. Non-issued uniform items that are not required for a particular assignment, i.e., chill-chaser jackets, knives, etc.
e. Personally-owned cellular and/or smart phones or electronic devices which may include, but not limited to, audio/video recorders, MP3 players, personal computers and mobile media devices.
f. Uniform clothing which becomes unusable as a result of normal wear.

5. When an article of clothing or issued equipment becomes unusable as a result of damage which occurs in the line of duty, the officer shall prepare an Equipment Replacement request form and forward the form through their chain of command. Once approved, the officer will take the approved request form and either take or send a photo of the damaged item to the Police Training Division where, if available, a replacement will be issued. If the item is not available, an order will be generated.

D. To replace an issued item as a result of loss or theft, the officer shall prepare an Equipment Replacement request with approval from their chain of command through the deputy chief and attach a copy of any applicable offense/incident report or inter-office correspondence and deliver to the Police Training Division.

1. If the lost or stolen equipment is subject to any type of insurance coverage payment, the officer shall reimburse the city for the replacement cost, up to the covered amount. Proof of insurance coverage shall be provided by the officer at the time of replacement through the Police Training Division. The Training Division shall forward the documentation to the Budget Section for appropriate action.
E. Replacement for portable radio batteries shall be made through the City Radio Services following approval through the appropriate chain of command.

F. On any other item of city-owned, non-expendable equipment which through normal use becomes unserviceable, the officer shall prepare an Equipment Replacement form and with approval of their chain of command deliver it to the Police Training Division for appropriate action.

Asset Management shall maintain uniform procedures for proper reporting, classification and control of fixed assets and all other department assets, owned or donated, to ensure that such assets are efficiently utilized and protected against damage and loss.

1. Fixed or Capital Asset - A fixed asset is a tangible item owned by the City with an original monetary cost of at least $10,000. Such items have an original life expectancy of greater than three (3) years and shall include land, buildings, equipment and improvements other than buildings.
a. Resource - Fixed assets over $10,000 or more.
b. Weapons, Equipment and Property (WEP) - All weapons, electronic devices, equipment and property over $1,000.
2. Mission Critical Management (MCM) - database utilized by Asset Management for the inventory of department assets that are $500 or more and three (3) or more years of usable life.
3. Land - A capital asset classification which includes all land purchases by or donated to the City. Donated land is recorded at its appraised value at the time of acquisition.

4. Buildings - A capital asset classification which includes all City-owned buildings and all permanently attached fixtures. If buildings are donated to the City, the value is recorded at its appraised value at the time of the acquisition.

5. Equipment - All tangible items owned by the City that are useful in carrying on operations. Examples may include, but are not limited to, machinery, tools, rolling stock, furniture and fixtures. Equipment donated to the City is recorded at estimated value.
6. Animals - All service animals are considered as fixed assets.
7. Eligible-equipment – Equipment that is required to be recorded in MCM database.

B. Asset Management will work with the Fleet Services, which shall be responsible for all vehicles and vehicle equipment, and with the City Radio Services Manager, who is responsible for maintaining all mobile and portable radios, to ensure all assets are entered into the MCM database.

C. When a purchase of a qualifying asset is approved by management, including grant-acquired property, the activity shall be reported to Asset Management by field personnel and/or Procurement Section staff.
1. Upon approval to purchase equipment or fixed asset, Police Finance staff will perform a budget review and assign a funding identifier (FID).
a. If funds from asset forfeiture, Crime Control and Prevention District, or grants are used, Police Finance will route the PAF to the appropriate section for additional details.
b. Once finalized, Police Finance staff will forward the PAF to Police Procurement.
2. Police Procurement staff will review the PAF, provide the Purchase Order (PO) number, and forward to Asset Management.
3. Field personnel will forward all P-card purchases for eligible equipment, machinery and weapons (purchased valued at $500 or more and three (3) or more years of usable life) to Asset Management.

4. In order to coordinate the recording and tagging of eligible equipment, delivery from vendor shall be coordinated with Asset Management. Whenever possible, the delivery of eligible equipment shall be to the warehouse dock at Bob Bolen Safety Complex (511 W Felix Street, Fort Worth, TX 76115). Asset Management will arrange pickup or delivery as appropriate.
D. Donations of Fixed Assets and/or Equipment
1. The guidelines for accepting gifts and donations, both cash and non-cash, are found in the City of Fort Worth Donations Policy.

2. Any and all non-cash donations which result in a capital asset as outlined within the City’s Capital Asset Policy shall be accepted following the procedures outlined in the City of Fort Worth Donation Policy.

3. No member of the department may accept any donation of fixed assets and/or equipment of any value that will result in the need of expenditure of other City funds or having a contractual obligation incurred by the City without approval of the City Council.
4. Monetary donations equal to or less than $5,000 may be received only by the Chief of Police.

This policy identifies the strategies and oversight concerning the appropriate use of federally controlled equipment. Federally controlled equipment is defined as only that equipment as outlined in this order and issued by the federal government or purchased with federal funds. The appropriate training, oversight, and documentation for the use of federally controlled equipment shall be adhered to as directed by Executive Order 13688 issued May 2015.
A. Definitions and Applications/Use - Federally Controlled Equipment
1. Manned Aircraft, Fixed Wing - Powered aircraft with a crew aboard, such as airplanes that use a fixed wing for lift.
a. Application/Use - Routine patrol, situational awareness and victim location/rescue operations.
2. Manned Aircraft, Rotary Wing - Powered aircraft with a crew aboard, such as helicopters that use a rotary wing for lift.
a. Application/Use - Routine patrol, situational awareness and victim location/rescue operations.
3. Unmanned Aerial Vehicles - A remotely piloted, powered aircraft without a crew aboard.
a. Application/Use - Aerial operations requiring low altitude or stationary flight operations, HAZ‐MAT, accident reconstruction, situational awareness, or operations posing a risk to human life.

4. Armored Vehicles, Wheeled - Any wheeled vehicle either purpose‐built or modified to provide ballistic protection to its occupants, such as a Mine‐Resistant Ambush Protected (MRAP) vehicle or an Armored Personnel Carrier. These vehicles are also referred to as Armored Rescue Vehicles (ARVs).

a. Application/Use - During operations where there is concern for officer or civilian safety, such as fugitive apprehensions, search warrant service, hostage rescue and barricaded subject operations. These vehicles provide ballistic protection and subsequently a higher level of safety for both officers and victims.

5. Tactical Vehicles, Wheeled - A vehicle purpose‐built to operate on and off road in support of military operations, such as a HMMWV (“Humvee”), 2.5‐ton truck, 5‐ton truck, or a vehicle with a breaching or entry apparatus attached.
a. Application/Use - Rough terrain or inclement weather for search and rescue operations, victim evacuations, disaster supply deliveries and emergency personnel transportation.
6. Command and Control Vehicles - Any wheeled vehicle either purpose‐built or modified to facilitate the operational control and direction of public safety units responding to an incident.
a. Application/Use - Serve as a centralized location for command decision-making, enhanced communication and other situational awareness capabilities.
7. Explosives and Pyrotechnics - Includes explosive breaching tools often used by special operations units.

a. Application/Use - Create a breach point opening in a structure during a hostage rescue operation or other high-risk entry. It may also include devices used to distract or temporarily disorient a suspect prior to law enforcement entry into a structure.

8. Breaching Apparatus - Tools designed to provide law enforcement rapid entry into a building or through a secured doorway. These tools may be mechanical in nature, such as a battering ram; ballistic such as slugs; or explosive.
a. Application/Use - To gain rapid entry into a structure that may be fortified or where a suspect refuses entry.

9. Riot Batons - Non‐expandable baton of greater length (generally in excess of 24 inches) than service‐issued types and are intended to protect officers during melees by providing distance from assailants. These batons offer a greater level of safety for officers by extending the distance between them and a violent or non‐compliant subject.
a. Application/Use - Deployed during demonstrations or civil disorder events.

10. Riot Helmets - Helmets designed to protect the officer’s face and head from injury during demonstrations or civil order events from projectiles including rocks, bricks, liquids, etc. Riot helmets include a visor which protects the face.
a. Application/Use - Worn by officers during demonstrations or civil disorder events where the threat or presence of dangerous projectiles is likely.

11. Riot Shields - Shields intended to protect officers from their head to their knees in demonstrations or civil disorder events. Most are designed for the protection of the officer from projectiles including rocks, bricks, and liquids. Some afford limited ballistic protection as well.

a. Application/Use - Utilized in conjunction with riot helmets to protect officers from projectiles and other hazards while trying to contain, move or disperse people during demonstrations or civil disorder events where the threat or presence of dangerous projectiles is likely.
B. Appropriate Use of Federally Controlled Equipment

1. Prior planning, to include the requirements for deployment and the level of supervisory approval necessary, should precede any use of federally controlled equipment. When, due to exigent circumstances, this is not possible and immediate use of the equipment is necessary for officer safety reasons or lifesaving operations, the involved officer(s) will make appropriate notification to their supervisor as soon as possible after the incident.

2. Any officer who will utilize federally controlled equipment, or any supervisor who authorizes the use of federally controlled equipment, will receive initial and recurring training that addresses the appropriate and safe use of such equipment, or certification when mandated by other local, state or federal law. Only personnel who have been properly trained may use departmentally-owned equipment, even when deployed in other jurisdictions. Authorization for use of equipment in other jurisdictions must be approved by the Chief of Police or designee(s).
1. Absent exigent circumstances, federally controlled equipment should only be utilized for previously approved purposes and with the appropriate level of supervision.

2. Proper deployment and accountability with supporting or neighboring agencies that may request the use of resources and capabilities of the department’s federally controlled equipment shall follow department guidelines and be properly documented.
1. With reports furnished through Asset Management, the Assistant Chief over the Finance and Personnel Bureau will evaluate the need for continued use of such equipment on an annual basis.

2. Following each deployment, an after-action report will be completed by the supervisor over the employee(s) using the federally controlled equipment that captures information such as the equipment utilized, the manner in which it was utilized, and the location of the utilization. This information shall be forwarded to and maintained by the Assistant Chief over the Finance/Personnel Bureau within five (5) days of use.

1. An internal auditing procedure shall be established by Asset Management to ensure that federally controlled equipment is being maintained and utilized as intended. This procedure will include provisions for accountability at the individual officer level to mitigate any misuse or unauthorized use. Such procedures will also support any reporting requirements.

1. The Fort Worth Police Department and its officers will actively engage the public to inform them of the purpose and intended use of federally controlled equipment. While maintaining operational security needs, personnel should explain the application of certain pieces of equipment and how its use will protect both citizens and officers.
2. Information regarding the cost realized by the department as a result of participation in such federally controlled equipment programs shall be provided if requested.

A. Inspections of the department shall be conducted on a regular basis to help ensure that the department is operating at peak efficiency and in compliance with established professional standards. When conducted properly, readiness inspections enable personnel to assess the department’s ability to perform its mission, provide the information necessary to plan for the improvement of departmental operations, and ensure full capability to perform the department’s mission.
B. Readiness Inspections will be conducted to evaluate both equipment and the operational readiness of the department to respond to exceptional or emergency circumstances.
1. Such inspections shall be regularly scheduled by the supervisor, but may be initiated at any time at the direction of the Chief of Police or designee.

2. Inspections include verification that all personnel have updated contact information available via the department portal in case of emergency call-back or notifications as required in General Order 211.01, Employees’ Home Addresses and Telephone Numbers.

1. Equipment readiness is the capability of any given piece of equipment to function in the intended manner at any given time. Informal inspections will be conducted on all department special-use equipment on a monthly basis.

2. Each departmental unit will create a checklist of equipment from the unit’s asset inventory list that is for special or periodic use and assign a position to conduct the monthly inspections. This position should be the same person responsible for the asset inventory list. Special or periodic-use equipment is typically equipment that is not assigned to individual members of the department. Special-use equipment includes, but is not limited to, special-use vehicles, equipment, supplies for special events or disasters, or specialized investigative equipment.
a. Checklists should indicate the unit, date inspected, condition of each item, and the person who inspected the equipment. Any maintenance needs will be identified.
b. Information should be consistent with the Division’s asset inventory described in General Order 509.02, Replacement of Equipment.

3. A formal quarterly report shall be generated based on each unit’s checklist and forwarded by the supervisor through their chain to the applicable Deputy Chief for review. Once approved by the Deputy Chief, the entire report or a signed IOC stating the inspection has been completed and equipment is in good condition will be forwarded to Policy Management and Safety for appropriate filing with the Texas Recognition Program. It is the bureau’s discretion to maintain the entire report in either the division or bureau files.

1. Supervisors shall daily conduct roll call inspections of all officers in their command to ensure availability and serviceability of equipment, personal appearance, and proper uniforms. Daily inspections include, but are not limited to, observance that:
a. Officers’ uniforms and equipment are clean, complete, and in good order.
b. Officers are in compliance with General Order 502.01, Hair and Mustache.
c. Officers are properly equipped and attired in keeping with their prescribed duty assignment.
d. Any missing, damaged or malfunctioning equipment is reported and, if necessary, investigated.
e. All property owned or controlled by the department, whether for general purposes or for use by individual members, is cared for and used properly.
f. Whether or not practices or procedures are being properly performed.
g. A situation which has the potential for creating a hazardous or life-threatening environment to employees or citizens is corrected immediately.

2. At least once a month, the Commander/Captain shall ensure supervisors conduct a formal Roll Call formation of their officers. Supervisors shall document the inspection and forward the report through their chain to the applicable deputy chief for their review. Additionally, the monthly report that falls at the end of a quarter shall be forwarded to Policy Management and Safety for appropriate filing with the Texas Recognition Program. It is the bureau’s discretion to maintain the entire report in either the division or bureau files.
a. The supervisor shall inspect the uniform, including the uniform hat, the personal appearance of the officer, and the functionality of:
b. This inspection meets the requirement of General Order 501.01G.

3. The monthly roll call formation shall include all specialized units to ensure uniform and equipment readiness. Officers working in an undercover assignment can bring their uniform and standard equipment to a secured location for inspection.

4. Supervisors shall at all times maintain constant vigilance of uniformed/non-uniformed personnel and take corrective action when necessary to address any officer’s personal appearance and/or uniform or non-unformed attire not in conformity with departmental requirements.

5. It is the responsibility of every Fort Worth Police Department supervisor to correct such circumstances immediately where failure to do so will jeopardize the Fort Worth Police Department’s reputation, its policies and procedures, and/or the accomplishment of the department’s mission.
